articles.full_text:
Chinese tech platform Channel Gate is reporting that Nvidia is soon to transition from 6GB to 24GB models for the RTX 5080, following reports earlier in the month that the RTX 5090 was effectively discontinued - reports that Nvidia has since firmly denied. Interestingly, the RTX 5080 24GB could arrive in some markets as early as December this year, and effectively becomes the top GeForce GPU offering in a world where RTX 5090 cards are unaffordable and/or in extremely limited supply.
According to the ChannelGate report, the RTX 5080 16GB and RTX 5090 D V2 will no longer be supplied to Chinese retailers. The country currently has around two months' supply of RTX 5080 16GB units, so by December that supply should be essentially exhausted, neatly bookending the arrival of the new 24GB cards - which use the new 3GB GDDR7 memory modules that were previously expected to form the basis of a new RTX 50-Series Super lineup.
The timing here is still in flux, with the Channel Gate report suggesting that the December date is the earliest possible time the 24GB RTX 5080 could debut, while a more conservative timeframe would see the new GPU variant arrive in January 2027 instead.
Normally, the Chinese market precedes the global GPU market by a matter of weeks at most, so it's expected that the RTX 5080 24GB would arrive worldwide in a broadly similar timeframe rather than remaining as a China-exclusive product.
At present this report doesn't provide any hard evidence to substantiate its claims, but with January a terrifying two months away, we don't have too long to wait to see if they bear fruit.

Ukraine's Progress in Satellite Communications
According to Слово і Діло — Інфографіка: Satellite networks in Ukraine are rapidly advancing, highlighted by the successful deployment of the experimental OBRIA NANO satellite and the recent lifting of usage limits on Starlink and Starshield systems. Since 2022, the company HIMERA, specializing in secure tactical communication systems, has been a key player in this sector. On October 1, 2026, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket launched the OBRIA NANO satellite into orbit as part of the Transporter-18 mission. Prior to this, no public details about the OBRIA project were available until October 27, 2026.
A major milestone in Ukraine’s satellite industry was reached in April 2026 when Danish aerospace firm GomSpace signed an agreement to establish a joint venture within Ukraine for satellite manufacturing. GomSpace, founded in 2007, expanded its capabilities by acquiring the Swedish company NanoSpace in 2016.
Enhanced Military Capabilities Through Satellite Technology
Recently, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense confirmed the removal of speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield networks. This decision came after Elon Musk addressed concerns regarding the alleged misuse of these systems by Ukrainian armed forces. Removing these limits significantly boosts the potential for satellite technology applications in defense operations.
Even before the full-scale invasion, Ukraine demonstrated its commitment to homegrown satellite development with the launch of the 'Sich-2-30' satellite. Commenting on technological advancements, Serhiy Beskrestnov stated:
“The 'Rassvet' project will be capable of drone control within six months.” - Serhiy Beskrestnov
These developments signal notable progress in Ukraine’s satellite communications and related technologies.
Beyond military uses, Ukraine’s satellite advancements are crucial for communication, monitoring, and various civilian applications. Collaborations with international aerospace companies like GomSpace highlight growing global interest and investment prospects in Ukraine’s space technology sector. Amid ongoing security challenges, strengthening satellite infrastructure is poised to play a vital role in national defense and the country’s technological growth.

articles.title: Philippine enterprises urged to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption amid rising hardware costs and evolving cybersecurity risks - Manila Bulletin
articles.summary: Philippine enterprises urged to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption amid rising hardware costs and evolving cybersecurity risks  Manila Bulletin
articles.full_text:
Philippine enterprises must hasten their adoption of artificial intelligence to preserve their competitiveness in an increasingly technology-driven global marketplace, even as organizations navigate the realities of rising hardware expenses, heightened cybersecurity threats, and the complexities of legacy system modernization. This consensus emerged from technology industry leaders during the VST ECS CXO Tech Summit 2026, an executive gathering that convened representatives from major global technology firms to examine the future of enterprise information technology, digital transformation, and the mission-critical infrastructure required to power next-generation business operations. The discussions reflected a decisive industry shift away from treating artificial intelligence as a speculative, discretionary initiative toward recognizing it as a fundamental operational imperative that requires organizations to fundamentally realign their technology capital investments, operational strategies, and workforce competencies.
VST ECS Philippines President and Chief Executive Officer Jimmy Go acknowledged that the domestic market continues to trail several neighboring Southeast Asian countries in enterprise AI adoption, particularly in deploying specialized AI servers and the advanced infrastructure necessary to sustain them. Go noted that Singapore began realizing substantial commercial activity from AI server deployments roughly two years ago, followed by aggressive capital deployments in Malaysia and Thailand last year. “The Philippines is kind of late in this AI revolution,” Go said, noting that stronger AI implementation, data center development, and hyperscaler investments could become more evident locally in the coming years. Despite this lag, Go cautioned local leaders against delaying investments until AI technologies achieve absolute maturity, highlighting that enterprise information technology has evolved into a vital competitive differentiator rather than a discretionary overhead cost, placing organizations that defer modernization at a disadvantage against faster-moving competitors. Demonstrating this commitment internally, VST ECS has begun deploying AI across its own commercial operations, investing directly in dedicated AI server infrastructure and integrating advanced AI capabilities into its enterprise software applications.
A central theme across the summit focused on establishing robust, modernized foundations prior to rolling out sophisticated enterprise AI deployments.
Daryush Ashjari, APJ Chief Technology Officer and Vice President for Solution Engineering at Nutanix, illustrated the risks of mismatched architecture by comparing AI infrastructure to a high-performance supercar operating on a gravel road, pointing out that a vehicle’s elite capabilities remain inherently constrained by a subpar operational environment.
Ashjari emphasized that organizations implementing high-performance AI frameworks atop antiquated legacy platforms cannot fully realize their financial investments, urging enterprises to establish forward-looking modernization roadmaps that bridge existing setups with future AI workloads without necessarily replacing every legacy system overnight.
Reinforcing this measured perspective, Matthew Yeo, Global Engineering Technologist at Dell Technologies, highlighted the operational necessity of validating practical, tangible use cases prior to committing substantial capital to costly AI hardware.
Yeo revealed that fewer than ten of the initial four thousand AI solutions evaluated by his organization successfully advanced to full enterprise production, explaining that companies routinely stumble by acquiring servers, graphics processing units, and specialized software without establishing clear performance frameworks, measurable targets, or well-defined business objectives.
For small and medium enterprises operating with modest budgets, Yeo advised initiating small, targeted pilots, assessing the operational findings, and progressively scaling only the applications that deliver measurable value.

Compounding implementation challenges, the global appetite for AI hardware is exerting significant financial and logistical pressure across enterprise supply chains. Go warned that mounting worldwide demand for memory modules, solid-state drives, graphics processing units, and specialized silicon components has elevated pricing across diverse hardware categories, including laptops, mobile devices, enterprise servers, and storage solutions. Go acknowledged that while supply constraints are real and pricing trajectories remain difficult to predict, price pressures affect memory-heavy platforms and GPU servers more heavily than networking gear, with vendors still providing delivery estimates despite lengthened lead times. To navigate these rising capital barriers, Walter So, Managing Director at HPE, recommended that enterprises leverage flexible consumption models, such as private cloud environments that enable organizations to pay incrementally for the computing capacity they actually consume instead of funding massive hardware acquisitions upfront. In parallel, Harold Lim, Country Solutions Head at APC by Schneider Electric Philippines, stressed that organizations must evaluate critical physical infrastructure constraints, as modern AI clusters consume immense amounts of electrical energy and require specialized cooling architectures, including liquid cooling, to avoid operational disruption.
Digital security must also advance in lockstep with technological deployment, according to Bambi Escalante, Country Manager at Fortinet Philippines, who warned that cybersecurity should never be treated as an afterthought. Escalante stressed that enterprises moving from generative AI tools toward autonomous AI agents must proactively balance operational innovation with risk management, establishing visibility over shadow AI tools, assigning precise identities and role-based access permissions to autonomous agents, and enforcing zero-trust, continuous monitoring, and defense-in-depth principles. Pointing to threat intelligence recording approximately twenty thousand automated vulnerability scans per second, Escalante observed that cybercriminals are actively employing AI to automate attacks, meaning smaller firms can no longer consider themselves immune to targeting. Consequently, organizations must deploy AI-powered defensive capabilities to counteract increasingly automated and sophisticated threats.
Achieving meaningful enterprise returns also hinges on data hygiene and comprehensive workforce enablement. Go underscored that enterprises must first establish resilient underlying IT environments and systematically organize their proprietary data assets, warning that poorly managed data undermines an AI model’s ability to produce dependable business insights or automate corporate workflows. Addressing data sovereignty policies and local residency guidelines, Go expressed optimism that clear regulatory frameworks could incentivize broader investments in domestic data center ecosystems and sovereign cloud architectures. On the human capital side, Ida Ong-Co, Managing Director at HP Philippines, emphasized that technological investments fail without comprehensive employee enablement, discussing HP’s AI Academy initiative, which tailors training programs to an organization’s maturity level and extends digital instruction to educators so they can bring AI literacy into classrooms. Ong-Co urged corporate leaders to pivot their focus toward identifying measurable productivity gains and tangible business outcomes rather than pursuing AI adoption for its own sake.
To assist domestic enterprises in navigating this multifaceted technological landscape, VST ECS is broadening its solutions ecosystem and technical resources. Cherry Centeno, First Vice President and Group General Manager for Value Business at VST ECS Philippines, noted that the distributor has incorporated more than twenty additional specialized solutions into its portfolio while mobilizing over three hundred pre-sales and post-sales technical engineers to assist clients with enterprise solution architecture and deployment. Centeno spotlighted the company’s dedicated experience and demonstration centers, as well as its proof-of-concept testing environments, which allow organizations to simulate infrastructure configurations and evaluate practical viability before allocating full capital expenditure. While the Philippines is navigating its enterprise AI investment cycle later than regional counterparts, industry leaders noted that local enterprises possess an advantageous opportunity to study early deployments elsewhere, bypass costly experimentation, and implement tested use cases. Moving forward, the true gauge of AI success across Philippine business will center on how effectively organizations weave these capabilities into core operations to deliver sustainable efficiency, competitive advantage, and measurable business value.

articles.title: AI-Native GCCs: How Artificial Intelligence is Reshaping Talent, Technology and Operating Models - Analytics Insight
articles.summary: AI-Native GCCs: How Artificial Intelligence is Reshaping Talent, Technology and Operating Models  Analytics Insight
articles.full_text:
Global Capability Centers (GCCs) are moving beyond their traditional roles as cost-efficient delivery hubs to become strategic centers for technology, product development, research, and innovation. Artificial intelligence is accelerating this transition, reshaping workforce composition, technology architecture, organizational structures, and decision-making. However, moving from AI experimentation to enterprise-wide impact remains a challenge. Dipanwita Ghosh, Head of Consulting at Embark, explains how GCCs can build AI-ready workforces, redesign operating models and establish the governance and technology foundations needed to scale AI-led innovation.
How is AI Reshaping Talent Mix and Organizational Structures Within GCCs?
AI will reshape GCC workforce composition before it materially changes overall headcount. Embark’s research suggests no single AI-era pyramid. In routine technology and transactional work, demand for junior execution and coordination will moderate through slower hiring, lower backfilling and role consolidation, not wholesale workforce reduction. In complex technology, ER&D, regulated operations and judgment-intensive enterprise functions, teams will retain greater depth as specialist expertise and experienced oversight gain weight.
A new capability layer will emerge across AI and data engineering, MLOps and AgentOps, platform and enterprise architecture, model validation and observability, AI governance, cybersecurity and human-in-the-loop exception orchestration. Equally important will be AI-enabled domain and process owners who can frame problems, redesign workflows, combine business context with AI and own outcomes end to end. Managers will shift from supervising tasks to governing exceptions, quality, adoption and human-agent collaboration.
At Embark, we help enterprises translate these shifts into organization design, role architecture, reskilling and hiring roadmaps. Over time, we expect new demand across AI, platforms, data, governance and domain-led transformation to offset much of the moderation in execution-heavy work, creating a more capability-dense workforce rather than a uniformly smaller one.
How is GCC Technology Architecture Changing to Support AI-Led Innovation and Scale?
An AI-native GCC requires an architecture that moves from disconnected copilots and proofs of concept to a reusable, governed system that can orchestrate complete workflows. Embark’s survey of 100 GCC leaders found that 92% are already beyond selective AI adoption, yet virtually all are realizing productivity gains of less than 15%. This suggests that access to models is not the principal constraint; execution readiness is.
The foundation is a governed data layer that connects structured and unstructured information with clear ownership, quality, lineage, privacy and access controls. Above it, GCCs need shared model and agent platforms, reusable services and APIs, and an integration layer that safely connects AI with enterprise applications, events, and human approvals. MLOps, LLMOps and AgentOps must support evaluation, deployment, observability, feedback and lifecycle management. Identity, cybersecurity, model risk, cost controls and auditability must be built in from the start.
The architecture must also capture value at the workflow level by measuring velocity, quality, released capacity, cost, and business impact. At Embark, we work backward from priority workflows to define the reference architecture and phased roadmap, helping clients move from task-level automation to scalable, trusted, end-to-end AI execution.
What Is Driving GCCs’ Shift from Execution Hubs to Strategic Centers?
Delivery credibility, access to capability, and the strategic importance of technology are driving the shift. Embark’s survey across GCC leaders found that deep technology and digital talent was the leading driver, followed by AI, data and automation capability and product, engineering and R&D capability. Cost efficiency emerges as a baseline, but no longer a sufficient reason to expand.
The progression is cumulative. Consistent execution builds enterprise trust; deeper capability enables ownership of products, platforms and functions; and proven outcomes unlock decision rights and selective global leadership roles in India. Enterprises are also internalizing strategic work and consolidating delivery into fewer capability centers because technology, AI, and intellectual property are too central to competitive advantage to remain purely transactional.
At Embark, we help enterprises determine which capabilities the GCC should own, establish leadership and decision rights, and design the required talent, technology and operating model. We also help launch AI and innovation centers of excellence where appropriate. A GCC becomes strategic when it owns roadmaps, decisions, and enterprise outcomes, not simply when its scale or title changes.
How is AI Transforming the Traditional GCC Operating Model?
AI is shifting the GCC operating model from task-based delivery to product, platform and value-stream ownership. Teams will increasingly combine human talent and AI agents across end-to-end workflows, with accountability for outcomes rather than activities. The first requirement is process redesign. Organizations must simplify hand-offs, define exception paths, and determine where AI can act, where humans must approve, and who remains accountable.
Governance should combine central control with distributed execution. Enterprise standards should govern approved models and tools, data access, security, model risk, testing, monitoring, cost and incident response, while domain teams innovate within those guardrails. In regulated or judgment-intensive work, human-in-the-loop review will remain essential for exceptions, overrides, and high-stakes decisions. As GCCs demonstrate control maturity and enterprise context, more decision authority can move closer to teams in India.
At Embark, we help clients map workflows, redesign roles and decision rights, establish governance forums and build deployment playbooks. We also shift measurement from tool adoption and FTE efficiency to workflow-level indicators such as velocity, quality, capacity released, risk reduction and business impact. Becoming AI-led ultimately redesigns how work is owned, governed, funded, and measured, not simply the introduction of new technology.
What Will Distinguish Successful AI-Native GCC, and What Should Leaders Prioritize?
A successful AI-native GCC will be distinguished by the depth of AI integration, not the number of tools or pilots it launches. In a conventional GCC, AI may improve productivity while the underlying workflow, governance, and decision model remains unchanged. In an AI-native GCC, AI is embedded in core processes and decisions, teams are organized around human-agent workflows, reusable platforms support deployment, and scaled solutions have clear ownership, controls, and measurable economics.
Embark’s research points to five priorities that must mature together: a governed data foundation; redesigned, AI-ready workflows; trusted deployment with security, auditability and human accountability; enterprise adoption supported by role redesign and AI fluency; and value measurement across speed, quality, cost, capacity released and business outcomes. Weakness in any one area will limit the move from pilots to scaled execution.
Leaders should begin with high-value workflows, prove outcomes quickly and scale through reusable patterns. Reinvest productivity gains into product, engineering, innovation, and ownership capabilities rather than treating them only as a headcount lever. Embark connects these decisions across the GCC lifecycle - from strategy and build through operations and transformation - so AI becomes part of the center’s operating system, not an overlay on the existing model.

articles.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11223-xPseudo-direct bandgap character in bismuth sulfide retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination while preserving strong light absorption.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation3—results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few kBT above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors4. The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Charge-carrier recombination in semiconductors is a fundamental process determining device efficiencies for a variety of key optoelectronic applications, ranging from photovoltaics5,6 to light-emission7,8 and photo(electro)catalysis9,10. Several intrinsic (for example, bimolecular) and extrinsic (for example, trap-mediated) recombination mechanisms contribute to charge-carrier recombination in light-harvesting devices such as photovoltaic and photochemical cells, in which recombination competes with charge-carrier extraction5,6,11 and thus causes efficiency losses. For any solar absorber material, minimizing extrinsic recombination losses is therefore a powerful first-line strategy to increase power conversion efficiencies12, with any remaining intrinsic losses defined by the detailed balance limit. For example, the benign defect chemistry of lead halide perovskites13 and the use of molecular passivation strategies12 have achieved trap-mediated recombination rates as low as k1 ≈ 105 s−1 (refs. 7,8). As a result, power conversion efficiencies of perovskite solar cells now reach values of about 28% (ref. 14). Similarly, more established technologies based around silicon or III–V semiconductors are reaching their intrinsic performance limits14,15 in solar devices.
These rapid developments mean that further minimization of charge-carrier recombination is now mostly hampered by Planck’s law, which sets inherent limitations to the reduction of intrinsic bimolecular electron–hole recombination rates4,16. In lead halide perovskites, similar to GaAs and Si, the intrinsic bimolecular recombination process of photogenerated electrons with holes is an inverse absorption process and has been demonstrated to follow the van Roosbroeck–Shockley (vRS) relation closely3,4,17,18. Therefore, the high bimolecular recombination rates reported for lead halide perovskites (LHP) and GaAs11,19 (k2,LHP ≈ 10−9 cm3 s−1, k2,GaAs ≈ 10−10 cm3 s−1) are a direct consequence of their direct bandgap character and the ensuing high absorption coefficients, which, taken on their own, are a desirable property for solar absorber materials. However, the associated high bimolecular recombination rates severely limit applications of perovskites and other highly absorbing semiconductors not only in solar cells but also in photoelectrocatalytic cells9,10. In these applications, extended charge-carrier lifetimes at semiconductor–electrolyte interfaces are vital for solar energy conversion to chemicals20.
Although the generalized Planck’s law sets a strict dependency between absorption and charge-carrier recombination efficiencies, these considerations apply only when both these processes originate from the same electronic state3. Decoupling light absorption and charge-carrier recombination processes is, therefore, a promising strategy to improve solar conversion efficiencies. This decoupling has generally been achieved only by sacrificing a considerable fraction of the photovoltage. Natural photosynthetic systems, for instance, trade around 0.7 eV in photovoltage to increase charge-carrier recombination lifetimes by six orders of magnitude20. A similar approach has been proposed in photoelectrochemical cells using polaron and electronic defect states in inorganic semiconductors, yet these strategies profoundly disrupt charge-carrier transport and, hence, increase efficiency losses substantially9,21,22. By contrast, Rashba splitting (that is, a spin–orbit-induced splitting in the k-space) has been proposed as a potential mechanism that could impart an indirect character to perovskites and thus yield long charge-carrier lifetimes23. However, several works demonstrated the direct bandgap nature of bulk halide perovskites and revealed the negligible part played by Rashba-related effects in recombination4,24,25,26, therefore leaving the quest for delayed recombination in semiconductors open.
Here, we show that bimolecular electron–hole recombination dynamics in Bi2S3 thin films deviate from the standard predictions of vRS theory for either direct or indirect semiconductors. By combining experimental and computational approaches, we determine the absorption properties of Bi2S3 and reveal a mixed direct–indirect bandgap character. We demonstrate that this peculiar electronic band structure, with a lowest-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed only a few tens of meV above, profoundly influences charge-carrier recombination in Bi2S3. Our temperature-resolved study of electron–hole recombination in Bi2S3 shows that the thermal equilibrium between direct and indirect transitions governs bimolecular recombination in this material. As a result, Bi2S3 offers an ideal combination comprising the best properties of both indirect and direct semiconductors, that is, retarded electron–hole recombination and high absorption coefficients, while sacrificing only minute potential photovoltage losses. Therefore, we propose Bi2S3 as the first candidate for a new and long-sought type of semiconductor—pseudo-direct semiconductors—which hold the potential to deliver efficient solar energy conversion.

We focus on bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3), an emerging non-toxic and stable semiconductor with promising photocatalytic, photodetector and energy-harvesting performance and an absorption onset at about 1.
4 eV, ideal for single-junction photovoltaics27,28,29.
We fabricated Bi2S3 thin films by thermal evaporation of Bi2S3 powders on ST-cut quartz substrates30.
As shown in Fig.
1a, Bi2S3 crystallizes in the orthorhombic stibnite structure (Pnma), which comprises parallel quasi-one-dimensional (Bi4S6)n ribbons bound by strong van der Waals interactions31.
The bandgap character of Bi2S3 is debated in the literature, with several experimental and theoretical studies of Bi2S3 stipulating both direct and indirect bandgap nature29,32,33,34.
Although recent work suggests the indirect bandgap nature of Bi2S3 (ref.
32), the reported high absorption coefficients (above 105 cm−1) cannot originate from indirect transitions35, which are substantially weakened by the requirement of phonon contributions to bridge momentum space.
To determine the nature of the Bi2S3 bandgap, we performed first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT)36,37 (Fig.
1b, Methods and Supplementary Information).
Our calculations indicate that several bands and valleys of Bi2S3—around the Γ, X and Z points of the Brillouin zone for the valence band and around Γ and Z for the conduction band—are closely spaced in energy by up to 2kBT and 7kBT for the valence and conduction band edges, respectively, where T is room temperature.
These multiple band extrema give rise to several energetically closely spaced direct and indirect transitions, as shown in Extended Data Fig.
1a, which probably fuelled the debate and contradictory claims in the literature around the nature of the bandgap in Bi2S3.

Despite a high absorption coefficient (α > 105 cm−1 for visible light), the absorption spectrum for Bi2S3 thin films at room temperature (Fig. 1c) lacks a sharp onset, similar to what is observed for AgBiS238, NaBiS239 and other bismuth-based semiconductors40,41. Although this gradual absorption onset resembles that of a prototypical indirect semiconductor (scaling as E2) more than that assumed for a direct semiconductor (scaling as E0.5, assuming parabolic bands), the values of the absorption coefficient are too high to be compatible with an indirect absorption process35. Through our first-principles calculations of Bi2S3, we show how the computed optical absorption spectrum (see the Supplementary Information for details) shown in Fig. 1d, which includes only contributions from direct transitions, exhibits a gradual onset with a similar line shape to that of the measured absorption coefficient. This comparison suggests that direct transitions form substantive components of the measured absorption. articles.title: The US space industry will suffer for Ukraine’s Starlink outage, experts say - Defense One
articles.summary: The US space industry will suffer for Ukraine’s Starlink outage, experts say  Defense One
articles.full_text:
US allies aren’t happy: “We naturally insist that it works if we're paying for it."
Elon Musk’s decision to hobble satellite services to Ukraine’s military, and his shifting explanations for doing so, have undermined the U.S. space industry and the country’s diplomatic and intelligence partnerships, say lawmakers, foreign officials, and former senior members of the U.S. military.
“I'm an American. You're an American. We want American companies to be the most competitive,” said one former senior military official who worked in space policy, operations, and acquisitions. Episodes like the Starlink scandal “create an environment where you make more competitors.”
On Oct. 14, amid a Russian missile barrage, military operators across Ukraine found themselves unable to direct drones traveling faster than 100 mph, causing “the failure of several missions,” Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook. Without warning, Musk’s SpaceX had imposed limitations on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military-grade data network that runs on the company’s Starlink constellation. The service reduction, which lasted ten days, reduced Ukraine’s ability to fend off Russian missiles and jet-powered drones.
“People were killed because [there was] not enough destruction, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work, of course," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said later on Oct. 14.
It’s not clear why SpaceX reduced service to Ukraine. Musk and President Donald Trump have been increasingly critical of Zelenskyy in recent weeks. Trump, who has reversed war-related sanctions on Russia and sought Moscow’s help to bring down domestic fuel prices, has complained about Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy plants. Musk, whose relationship with Kyiv has soured since the departure of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, has asked for sympathy for Russian conscripts.
Musk, who promised last year that “Starlink will never turn off its terminals” in Ukraine, blamed Trump for the slowdown.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he tweeted on Oct. 14.
That didn’t smell right to at least one former U.S. general.
“I honestly believe Musk thought he was acting in line with what the White House wanted. I can’t prove that, of course. But all the actions and everything people say tell me this was intentional,” said Ben Hodges, a retired general and former commander of U.S. Army Europe.
The inability to rely on SpaceX is sure to affect military decisionmaking, the former senior military official who worked in space policy said.
“From a planner perspective, obviously, you need to have confidence in your kill-chain capabilities, and so that introduces doubt, which must be incredibly difficult for the planners of the Ukrainian military.”
Congress’ concerns
In letters to SpaceX and the Pentagon, U.S. lawmakers expressed several concerns about the interruption of service, including its effects on allies.
On Oct. 19, a group of senators reminded SpaceX officials of their “contract obligations with the Federal Republic of Germany, which funds Ukraine’s access to Starlink,” and asked: “When did you notify the German government of the decision to degrade Starlink capabilities?”
Representatives from their offices did not respond to questions regarding any answer they may have received.
In an Oct. 22 letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, another group of senators noted that Ukraine relies on Starlink for intelligence-sharing. They urged the Pentagon to “expand its existing Starshield contract to ensure Ukraine has the satellite communications capacity, coverage, and reliability necessary to sustain its military operations and renew Starshield’s unlimited-speed service.” Pentagon officials did not respond to questions about the letter.
Allied government officials also expressed alarm.
"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision or group of people took this decision against a country that is literally fighting for the lives of the citizens against naked aggression," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Oct. 23.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Oct. 16 put the issue plainly: "Germany is paying SpaceX and that's why we naturally insist that it works if we're paying for it."
Facing mounting pressure, Trump called Musk on Oct. 23 to ask him to lift the restrictions.
On Friday, Trump said, “If there’s a problem, I'll get it straightened out.”
That same day, Musk admitted that SpaceX had put a speed restriction in place but he blamed Ukraine, which he said had used the satellite network for offensive drone strikes and thereby “violated Starlink terms of service and [the military] used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.” Ukrainian leaders have denied this.
But as the Oct. 19 letter points out, any real or imagined Starlink terms-of-service violation should not affect the Starshield service, which is under the control of the U.S. government. Like many, the senators were confused.
“SpaceX owns and operates the underlying Starlink network and infrastructure upon which certain Starshield services rely. These circumstances raise important questions...”
By Oct. 24, Ukrainian leaders said, full Starlink service had been restored.
What next?
For Ukrainian operators, the issue is resolved for now. But one former senior military official who worked in space systems acquisition told Defense One that the episode will undermine trust in U.S. satellite capabilities.
“Flipping the switches over a combat operation, it’s definitely a significant data point… The question is: Are we making the right decisions?”
U.S. dominance in space-based imaging and satellite communications, both military and commercial, is real. Europe does not have either a private or public satellite communications system capable of replacing Starlink overnight. Starlink’s importance in helping Ukraine achieve battlefield gains is also beyond dispute.
But Musk’s actions will accelerate the development of foreign alternatives to Starlink, said the formal official. More established, smaller competitors to Starlink, such as Eutelsat OneWeb, SES, Iridium and others, could also see increased government business or support.
It’s not the first time that a U.S. decision to withhold satellite services has convinced a security partner to reduce its reliance on Washington. In 1999, India was denied access to GPS during its Kargil conflict with Pakistan.
“The request that was denied to India drove them to build their own GNSS [global navigation satellite system] capability,” the former official said.
The European Union launched its own quest for a navigation system that same year, and the Galileo navigation system went operational in 2016.
From the perspective of U.S. space firms, “You risk your momentum by giving other competitors a reason to go build their own Galileo GPS system,” the former official said.
The urgent need for sovereign satellite capability led Kyiv to sign a development agreement with Denmark’s GomSpace in April and, on Oct. 22, a letter of intent with Finnish space technology company ICEYE and Nokia.
For U.S. military operations, that’s not all bad news, the official said, as it means a more resilient network with more providers of services such as global positioning and communications.
But the United States will never again enjoy a position of near-dominance in space, they said.
“Your Apple iPhone right now takes in GPS, Russian GNSS, and Chinese GNSS, yeah. So, in one way, it makes your system more resilient. In other ways your little phone is reliant on other things, systems that probably we would not have planned to be reliant on many years ago.”

articles.title: Two weeks before Starlink’s speed cap hit Ukraine’s drones, a Ukrainian test satellite went up on a SpaceX rocket - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: Two weeks before Starlink’s speed cap hit Ukraine’s drones, a Ukrainian test satellite went up on a SpaceX rocket  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
A test satellite for a future communications network under Ukrainian control is working in orbit, Ukraine’s Himera and Denmark’s GomSpace said on 27 October. The companies say it will work for Ukraine’s strategic security, and that the long-term aim is to rely less on foreign communications providers. Public launch records for the mission do not list a satellite by that name, though some of its objects are still unidentified.
Ukraine fights Russia on satellite links it doesn’t control, and the announcement comes two weeks after it saw what depending on an outside provider can cost. The satellite, the companies say, went up on 1 October, before that trouble began. Overnight on 14 October, Starlink and its military version, Starshield, began dropping links on fast-moving terminals, and Ukrainian officials said the cap disrupted drone missions. On 24 October, 10 days after the cap began, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported speeds restored. Who ordered the cap remains contested. That same day, Elon Musk wrote that Ukraine’s military had violated Starlink’s terms of service and that “that loophole was closed last week,” a claim a Ukrainian presidential adviser disputed.
What the companies say, and what launch records show
Obria Nano flew on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission, the release said. Aalborg-based GomSpace built it on Himera’s order, Himera co-founder and CEO Misha Rudominski wrote on Facebook. He added that the team received the first signals the next day and that the satellite is now working. Its tests are meant to inform the design of the full Obria system, the release said.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays
No satellite called Obria Nano appears on SpaceX’s published list for the mission, The Insider found. Public tracking catalogs show one Ukrainian satellite from that launch, named UASAT-Nano. Another 26 objects from the mission are still listed with placeholder names and no confirmed owner. The outlet said it is unclear whether the two names refer to one satellite.
UASAT-Nano is the satellite network Stetman, another Ukrainian company, is building, and its founder said the network’s first test satellite would launch in October. In April, Stetman and GomSpace agreed to set up a joint venture called UASAT and planned a first launch for fall 2026. The Obria release does not mention Stetman or UASAT.
Production in Ukraine is the stated next step
Rudominski wrote that Himera’s next stage is to produce satellites and ground terminals in Ukraine. He called it important not only to use the technology but also to gradually build domestic expertise and manufacturing.
“For us, this project is about more than launching a satellite. It is an opportunity to lay the foundation for an independent communications network for Ukraine,” Rudominski said in the release.
In the long run, the network would cover all of Ukraine and complement European satellite networks, the release said. The network does not exist yet, and Himera has given no timeline.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
Replacing Starlink will not be quick. Lance Hunter, a political scientist at Augusta University, told Time that Ukraine cannot quickly swap out such technology, since diversifying it “takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources.” Meanwhile, one Ukrainian interceptor-drone maker has begun rethinking its air-launched designs after the slowdown.

articles.title: Two Russian Starlink Rival Satellites Are Now Set to Fall from Orbit - 19FortyFive
articles.summary: Two Russian Starlink Rival Satellites Are Now Set to Fall from Orbit  19FortyFive
articles.full_text:
Russia wants its own rivals to Starlink. Gravity, however, has other plans. Two satellites from Russia’s Rassvet broadband constellation, the Kremlin’s answer to SpaceX, are expected to burn up in the atmosphere after failing to raise their orbits, the Defence Blog reported this week.
Harvard-Smithsonian astrophysicist and satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell said most of the remaining Rassvet-3 satellites have settled at about 500 km.
These two never got there.
They’ve sunk below 230 km and are dropping fast.
Two dead satellites out of 32 doesn’t sound like much.
However, this is the second and third loss for a program that is already far behind schedule, and it says a lot about where Russia’s space industry stands in 2026.
Two Satellites That Never Left The Parking Lot
Both failing spacecraft came from the second batch of 16 Rassvet-3 satellites that Bureau 1440 launched on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on July 19.
The plan was simple enough.
The rocket drops the satellites into a low deployment orbit of roughly 300 km, and each one uses its own plasma thrusters to climb to its working altitude of over 500 km.
These two never fired.
By late August, the Defence Blog, citing Anatoly Zak of RussianSpaceWeb, reported that the pair had slipped below 300 km without a single orbit-raising maneuver.
The whole July batch was sluggish. At a similar stage, none of the 16 had climbed above 360 km, about 200 km lower than the first group managed.
The two satellites are tracked as RASSVET-3 17 and RASSVET-3 23. Ukrainian outlet UNN reported reentry forecasts of October 29 and November 1.
Analysts quoted by UNITED24 Media have pointed to a likely propulsion failure.
Bureau 1440, Roscosmos, and the Russian military have said nothing official about either doomed satellite.
This isn’t the program’s first casualty.
The Defence Blog reported back in June that a satellite from the March batch, cataloged as Object 4, reentered on June 6 without ever performing a maneuver.
Three satellites lost, none of them to anything more exotic than engines that never fired.
The Math Doesn’t Work
Russia’s real problem is the gap between what Moscow promised and what’s in orbit.
Bureau 1440, owned by IKS Holding since it was transferred from MegaFon a month after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, laid out an ambitious plan in July.
The company wants 156 Rassvet satellites in orbit by the end of 2026, 292 by 2027 when partial service is supposed to start, 610 by 2028 and 900 by 2035.
According to Orbital Radar’s Rassvet tracker, as of October 13, 31 production satellites were in orbit, and only 22 had reached their working altitude of about 510 km.
For those keeping score at home, that’s 31 against 156 with two months left in the year. And it’s about to be 29.
The altitude is a story by itself.
Rassvet was originally designed to operate at around 800 km.
TechRadar reported that Bureau 1440 paused raising some satellites toward that goal and never said why.
The constellation is now settling closer to 500 km.
Lower orbits mean more atmospheric drag, which requires more fuel to stay aloft and shortens service lives.
The Institute for the Study of War assessed that the July satellites will likely wear out faster than planned.
By contrast, SpaceX launches dozens of Starlink satellites at a time, several times a month.
Russia is launching 16 at a shot and losing some of them on arrival.
This Was Always About The Battlefield
Bureau 1440 sells Rassvet as a commercial 5G-from-orbit broadband service. Nobody in Kyiv buys that, and most analysts don’t either.
Starlink has been a game changer in Ukraine.
It keeps drone teams, artillery spotters, and command posts talking when everything else is jammed or blown up.
Russian units spent a long time using smuggled Starlink terminals of their own.
When ISW cut off that unauthorized access in February, it reported that Moscow accelerated Rassvet’s deployment.
A finished network could support battlefield communications and remotely controlled strikes against Ukraine.
The Rassvet deployments have begun to do that.
The Kyiv Post, citing a Ukrainian satellite communications expert, reported that by the end of July Rassvet was providing at least two communication windows a day over Ukraine, each lasting more than an hour.
While it’s nowhere near the always-on coverage Ukrainian troops get from thousands of Starlink satellites overhead, it does count.
However, that gap matters in a drone war.
A two-hour window works for scheduled data dumps.
It doesn’t work for a pilot steering an FPV drone or a long-range strike drone into a target at night, when the window is closed.
So why push so hard on a system that clearly isn’t ready?
Because Moscow has no other option. It can’t buy what SpaceX sells, and it can’t steal it anymore.
Russia Is Stuck With A System That Isn’t Ideal
Building a low Earth orbit constellation isn’t easy.
SpaceX lost satellites early too. Most of the Rassvet satellites are working, and 22 have reached their operating altitude.
Russia will keep launching, and Ukraine’s planners would be foolish to write the program off.
However, Russia is doing this under sanctions, with a launch rate that can’t come close to its own targets and a satellite builder that apparently can’t guarantee its thrusters will even fire.
Like so many Russian military programs, it is long on promises but short on actual delivery.
Every lost satellite is one more the factory has to replace before it can add a new one.
The 2027 service date is fantasy now, and the 2026 target died a while ago.
Russia wanted its own Starlink.
Right now, it has 29 satellites and two shooting stars.

A Singapore-based data center executive reportedly funneled information to Beijing while maintaining ties to Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia Corp. NVDA.
U.S. officials determined that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to a New York Times report on Thursday. Officials had previously suspected Huang was helping China circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips. Subsequent surveillance allegedly indicated she was also transmitting information directly to Beijing.
The surveillance reportedly documented a close relationship between Huang and Jensen Huang, raising questions about whether she obtained insight into Nvidia’s operations or U.S. policy toward China.
A Chinese businesswoman and investor, Ms. Huang, rose to a senior position at Megaspeed, a company suspected by U.S. officials of helping China circumvent export restrictions to access Nvidia computing power. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed in late 2024 after an inspection of its Malaysian data center found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, raising suspicions about how the chips were being handled.
President Donald Trump received a briefing about the intelligence findings about one year ago but decided against taking action. Officials reportedly believed intervention could disrupt chip sales and broader trade relations with China, according to the report.
Companies connected to Huang continued purchasing Nvidia chips this year, the report added.
An Nvidia spokesperson said in an email statement to Benzinga that, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” The spokesperson added, “The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.”
The spokesperson said its regional cloud customers receive "ordinary business information" rather than "sensitive Nvidia trade secrets," adding that they receive "zero information relevant to national security." The spokesperson noted that the company was confident the U.S. government would alert it if any person posed a threat to American industry. Nvidia also said it regularly receives government updates about "parties and entities of concern" and "always act[s] accordingly."
White House did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.
Nvidia’s China Exposure Faces Fresh Scrutiny
The findings add new scrutiny to Nvidia’s China exposure after short-seller Culper Research alleged in May that Singapore-based Megaspeed International, identified as Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer, is secretly financed by Alibaba Group Holding BABA through shell companies. The report also alleged close ties between Megaspeed’s leadership and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Culper further linked Megaspeed to a suspected server-smuggling network, citing the March 2026 DOJ indictment involving Super Micro Computer Inc. SMCI and OBON Corp. The firm describes Megaspeed as the "tip of the iceberg" and flagged Aivres Systems, formerly blacklisted Inspur Systems, as a potential China-focused supply channel, raising concerns about Nvidia’s revenue exposure and the diversion of AI chips to China.
Earlier this month, Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun, a contractor for Super Micro Computer, pleaded guilty to helping illegally export Nvidia AI chip-powered servers to China as part of an alleged $2.5 billion scheme.
In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) invited Jensen Huang to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about Nvidia’s U.S. export-control position and China operations. Warren argued that while Chinese purchases generate profits for American companies, they could undermine U.S. national security.

articles.title: European Commission grants €319m funding for next-generation semiconductors - Innovation News Network
articles.summary: European Commission grants €319m funding for next-generation semiconductors  Innovation News Network
articles.full_text:
€319m in Austrian state aid is being granted to Infineon Technologies to upgrade its semiconductor factory.
The factory is set to receive a €1.1bn upgrade, creating what it claims is the world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-generation semiconductors.
These are gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors on 300mm wafers, something Infineon says it was the first company to achieve in 2024.
GaN semiconductors are becoming increasingly important
Since 2024, these semiconductors have been used more and more as they replace silicon in power electronics. They can handle higher voltages, switch faster, and operate at higher temperatures, all while using less energy.
Current uses include device chargers, AI data centres, electric vehicles, solar panels, wind turbines, 5G and 6G telecoms base stations, and robotics.
Their wafers are larger than the standard 200mm wafers, which allows for 2.3x more individual chips to be made per wafer and lowers manufacturing costs.
The European Commission will now fund Infineon to scale up production of these chips. In its announcement on 28 October, the measure falls under the EU’s Chips Act, and will “strengthen the EU’s position and autonomy in the semiconductor value chain.”
The Chips Act aims to boost the EU’s share of global semiconductor production from 10% in 2023 to 20% by 2030, while increasing domestic suppliers and demand for European-made chips.
Infineon, which currently holds a 29% market share in the power systems sector and 50% in the automotive chips sector, says this investment and factory upgrade in Villach will turn the facility into a “global competence centre for power semiconductors”.
“A strong commitment to Austria”
Christian Stocker, the Austrian chancellor, said: “This is not only a strong commitment to Austria as a business location but also helps ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry will not be shaped solely in Asia or the United States, but also in Austria and Europe.”
Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies AG, added: “This substantial investment shows our clear commitment to strengthening the European semiconductor ecosystem and Europe’s technological sovereignty. By establishing high-volume manufacturing on 300-millimetre wafers, we will be the first company in the world to bring gallium nitride power electronics into volume production.”
European policy is pushing to make more chips, including semiconductors, to reduce reliance on outside production and secure its business future. Dr. Luigi Capoani and Alberto Corso of the European Youth Think Tank wrote for INN about how the EU should approach this and what it needs to focus on to achieve the best results.

articles.title: Ukraine Launches First Test Satellite as It Seeks Starlink Alternatives - The Defense Post
articles.summary: Ukraine Launches First Test Satellite as It Seeks Starlink Alternatives  The Defense Post
articles.full_text:
Ukraine’s HIMERA and Denmark’s GomSpace have placed a test satellite into orbit for a planned sovereign communications network, as Kyiv seeks to reduce its reliance on SpaceX’s Starlink amid concerns over its dependence on an external provider for critical communications.
Launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on the Transporter-18 mission on October 1, the OBRIA Nano satellite is undergoing technical tests to inform the design of a constellation intended to provide communications coverage across Ukraine and complement European satellite networks.
The next phase will involve localizing satellite and ground-terminal production in Ukraine, developing domestic expertise and expanding manufacturing capabilities.
Founded in 2022, HIMERA develops secure tactical radios for military use in electronic warfare environments. GomSpace manufactures small satellites, communications payloads, and spacecraft subsystems.
“For us, this project is about more than launching a satellite. It is an opportunity to lay the foundation for an independent communications network for Ukraine,” HIMERA co-founder and CEO Misha Rudominski said.
Rudominski said the initial tests would help develop capabilities to strengthen Ukraine’s strategic security and reduce dependence on external communications providers.
GomSpace CEO Carsten Drachmann said the companies shared an ambition to “strengthen Ukraine’s independent communications capabilities and support its long-term security and economic development.”
OBRIA Nano or UASAT-NANO?
The announcement follows an April agreement between GomSpace and Ukrainian satellite communications company STETMAN to establish a joint venture called UASAT to develop a separate satellite communications initiative.
Both HIMERA and GomSpace identify October 1 as the launch date for OBRIA Nano. However, SpaceX’s official Transporter-18 mission manifest lists a Ukrainian satellite named UASAT-NANO, deployed during the same mission.
The matching launch date, GomSpace’s involvement in both initiatives, and their similar objectives raise the possibility that OBRIA Nano and UASAT-NANO are the same spacecraft operating under different names.
Neither GomSpace nor HIMERA has publicly clarified the relationship between OBRIA and UASAT or explained STETMAN’s role in the OBRIA initiative.
UASAT Constellation
The planned UASAT constellation is designed to operate in low Earth orbit at an altitude of approximately 550 kilometers (342 miles), with resilience against electronic warfare.
GomSpace is expected to manufacture the satellites initially, with production gradually shifting to Ukraine.
The initial deployment plan prioritizes secure government and military communications, with 30,000 to 50,000 terminals expected to be supplied in 2027. The network could eventually support up to 100,000 terminals per country and expand to allied nations.
The roadmap calls for 120 satellites by 2027, followed by more than 100 launches annually. These figures are planned targets rather than confirmed deployments.
Ukraine Seeks Alternatives to Starlink
The planned constellation is part of Ukraine’s broader push to develop domestic satellite communications capabilities and diversify its options for secure connectivity.
Ukraine has relied heavily on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network for battlefield communications since Russia’s 2022 invasion. The service supports military command, drone operations, and connectivity in areas where terrestrial infrastructure has been damaged or disrupted.
Temporary restrictions imposed in mid-October disrupted Ukrainian connectivity and affected drone operations, including efforts to intercept Russian attack drones.
A separate initiative involving Finnish companies ICEYE and Nokia also reflects Ukraine’s efforts to reduce reliance on external communications providers. The companies signed a letter of intent with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence on October 22 to explore cooperation on a sovereign satellite communications system.
The proposed system would use low Earth orbit satellites to provide secure communications for defense and other government missions. Its first satellites are expected to launch in 2028, although the agreement does not constitute a confirmed procurement order.

articles.title: New York enacts ban on ‘unsafe’ chatbot behavior with kids as states push AI regulation boundaries - Boston Herald
articles.summary: New York enacts ban on ‘unsafe’ chatbot behavior with kids as states push AI regulation boundaries  Boston Herald
articles.full_text:
By MARC LEVY
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — New York is enacting farther-reaching restrictions on companion chatbot behavior, as states increasingly move to protect children who use artificial intelligence, regulate how employers deploy AI systems and push developers to prevent an AI-caused catastrophe.
Legislation signed Wednesday by Gov. Kathy Hochul outlines a dozen definitions of “unsafe AI companion features” that will be prohibited when a companion chatbot interacts with a child under 18.
A violation could expose a chatbot developer to a lawsuit by the state attorney general’s office. Penalties could include monetary damages, shutting down the chatbot and destroying data. The law takes effect Jan. 1.
Hochul, in the thick of her reelection campaign, signed the bill amid growing warnings about the existential risks posed by the rapid development of AI technology and calls for bold action by a reluctant Washington.
With Congress doing little to regulate AI, state legislatures are packed with efforts to wield state consumer protection laws to make AI use more transparent and rein in chatbots and rogue AI frontier models.
New York and California are at the vanguard of such laws that also are targeting social media platforms.
In September, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring chatbot developers to assess a model’s risk to children, show how they tried to eliminate those risks and submit to an independent audit to determine whether they are complying with the law.
He also signed legislation to prohibit social media platforms from deploying addictive features for users under 16.
Meanwhile, eight states sued AI giant OpenAI earlier this month, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what one activist called “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”
However, governors acknowledge that Congress and the federal government have farther-reaching abilities to clamp down on AI-posed threats, even as President Donald Trump has brushed off concerns and warned states not to regulate AI.
Under New York’s law, outlawed chatbot behavior with children under 18 includes suggestions that the chatbot is a real person that has emotions, opinions or an actual relationship with the child. It also outlaws chatbot messages that use flattery, involve sexually explicit material or encourage secrecy or unhealthy behavior.
Jim Steyer, founder and CEO of watchdog group Common Sense Media, called New York’s law “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country.”
Justine Gluck, policy analyst at the Future of Privacy Forum, a nonprofit focused on data protection and AI governance, said the different regulatory approaches by California and New York could be models other states adopt after legislatures reconvene next year.
New York’s law, she said, underscores how quickly chatbot regulation is evolving, as states move beyond basic disclosures and crisis-response protocols to regulating the underlying design and operation of chatbots.
Still, several categories in New York’s law are broadly worded or undefined, Gluck said.
That raises questions, she said, about “where ordinary conversational responsiveness ends and prohibited behavior begins,” and could complicate how it is enforced.

EU Approves EUR319 Million Austrian Aid for Infineon's EUR1.1 Billion Villach Chip Upgrade
The European Commission has approved EUR319 million in Austrian state aid for Infineon Technologies, supporting a EUR1.1 billion upgrade of the company's factory in Villach, according to Euronews. The Commission announced the measure on Wednesday 28 October under the EU Chips Act, stating that it would help reinforce the bloc's position and autonomy across the semiconductor value chain.
The investment is intended to let Infineon expand output and set up what the company describes as the first high-volume manufacturing facility worldwide for next-generation gallium nitride power semiconductors built on 300-millimetre wafers. The EU is working to cut its dependence on semiconductor imports from other countries and to establish itself as a technology leader alongside the United States and China.
The bloc aims to raise its share of global semiconductor production from 10% in 2023 to 20% by 2030. The Chips Act also targets stronger demand for European-made chips and support for domestic suppliers seeking to scale up. Infineon said the investment would make its Villach site a global competence centre for power semiconductors.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker described the project as one of the largest single investments in the history of Austria's high-tech industry. He said it represented a strong commitment to Austria as a business location and would help ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry is shaped not only in Asia or the United States but also in Austria and Europe.
Infineon, a German company focused on power systems and automotive semiconductors, holds a 29% market share in the former segment and 50% in automotive chips. Chief Executive Jochen Hanebeck said the investment demonstrated the company's commitment to strengthening the European semiconductor ecosystem and Europe's technological sovereignty. He added that high-volume manufacturing on 300-millimetre wafers would make Infineon the first company worldwide to bring gallium nitride power electronics into volume production.
Infineon said it was the first company to successfully process 300-millimetre gallium nitride wafers in 2024. GaN power semiconductors are increasingly replacing silicon in power electronics because they can handle higher voltages, switch faster and withstand higher temperatures. They are used in chargers for smartphones, laptops and tablets, as well as in AI data centres, electric vehicles, solar panels, wind turbines, 5G and 6G telecoms base stations and robots, with their energy efficiency proving useful where reducing power consumption matters.
The 300-millimetre wafers are larger than conventional 200-millimetre versions, allowing 2.3 times more individual chips per wafer and lowering manufacturing costs. Analysts expect the GaN power semiconductor market to reach approximately $3.1 billion by 2031, with annual growth of around 35% between 2025 and 2031. Upgrades at the Villach site are expected to be completed in 2034.

articles.full_text:
The European Commission has approved Austria’s state-aid grant to Infineon Technologies to upgrade its existing semiconductor facility in Villach, Carinthia, and make it the world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next generation semiconductors.
The European Commission has approved €319 million in Austrian state aid for semiconductor giant Infineon Technologies to help fund a €1.1 billion upgrade of its factory in Villach. The investment will enable the company to ramp up production and establish what it says will be the world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-generation gallium nitride power semiconductors on 300-millimetre wafers.
The Commission said in its announcement on Wednesday 28 October that the measure, under the EU’s Chips Act, will help “strengthen the EU’s position and autonomy in the semiconductor value chain”. The bloc is seeking to reduce its reliance on semiconductor imports from third countries and establish itself as a technology leader alongside the US and China.
The EU aims to increase its share of global semiconductor production from 10% in 2023 to 20% by 2030. The Chips Act also seeks to boost demand for European-made chips and help domestic suppliers scale up.
Infineon says the investment will position its Villach site as a “global competence centre for power semiconductors”.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the project was “one of the largest single investments in the history of Austria’s high-tech industry”.
“This is not only a strong commitment to Austria as a business location but also helps ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry will not be shaped solely in Asia or the United States, but also in Austria and Europe,” he added.
Infineon, a German company specialising in power systems and automotive semiconductors, holds a 29% market share in the former sector and 50% in automotive chips.
“This substantial investment shows our clear commitment to strengthening the European semiconductor ecosystem and Europe’s technological sovereignty,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies AG.
“By establishing high-volume manufacturing on 300-millimeter wafers, we will be the first company in the world to bring gallium nitride power electronics into volume production,” he added.
A new kind of semiconductor
Infineon says it was the first company to successfully process 300-millimetre gallium nitride (GaN) wafers in 2024.
GaN power semiconductors are increasingly replacing silicon in power electronics because they can handle higher voltages, switch faster and tolerate higher temperatures.
They are used in chargers for smartphones, laptops and tablets, as well as in AI data centres, electric vehicles, solar panels, wind turbines, 5G and 6G telecoms base stations and robots. Their energy efficiency makes them particularly useful in applications where reducing power consumption is important.
The 300-millimetre wafers are larger than the conventional 200-millimetre versions, allowing 2.3 times more individual chips to be produced per wafer and lowering manufacturing costs.
Analysts expect the GaN power semiconductor market to reach approximately $3.1 billion by 2031, representing annual growth of around 35% between 2025 and 2031.
The upgrades to the Villach site are expected to be completed in 2034.

Key Takeaways
- The semiconductor supply chain spans chip design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution.
- Disruptions and capacity constraints can cause chip shortages and raise prices across industries.
- Companies and governments are expanding production and suppliers to strengthen chip availability.12
What Are Semiconductors?
Semiconductors are critical components found in modern electronics. They are used in a wide range of products, from smartphones and laptops to automobiles and medical devices. These include microprocessors, memory modules, and integrated circuits found in these and other devices.
The semiconductor supply chain refers to the network of companies involved in design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution. The supply chain is complex, involving the coordination of a number of different stages, from sourcing parts and materials to the sale to the final end user.
One of the primary reasons for the pandemic-era shortage of semiconductors was snags in the supply chain caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted production and shipping around the world. Lockdowns and other restrictions forced many workers to stay at home and semiconductor manufacturers to reduce their capacity or temporarily shut down production lines, while staffing shortages, quarantines, and port closures caused shipping delays that have slowed the distribution of chips. In its September 30, 2026 report, Micron identified AI-driven demand and insufficient memory production capacity as current pressures on memory chip supply.23
Why Semiconductors Matter to Today’s Economy
Semiconductors, also known as “semis,” or chips, are ubiquitous in modern technology and are used in a wide range of products such as computers, smartphones, cars, household appliances, gaming systems, and medical equipment. As a result, semiconductors are incredibly important for today’s economy because they drive innovation and productivity in many industries.
The technical definition of a semiconductor is a material (usually composed of silicon) that conducts electricity more than an insulator, such as glass, but less than a pure conductor, such as copper or aluminum. Their conductivity and other properties can be altered with the introduction of specific impurities, called doping, to meet the particular needs of the electronic component in which it resides.
The global semiconductor industry is a large and growing market, generating revenues of $574.1 billion in 2022.4 The industry is also a major employer, with hundreds of thousands of people working in the design, manufacturing, and distribution of semiconductors worldwide. Given their importance to the economy, semiconductors have become a key strategic industry sector for many countries, with governments and companies alike investing heavily in research and development to maintain competitiveness and innovate.
A Comprehensive Look at the Semiconductor Supply Chain
The semiconductor supply chain involves a complex network of companies, organizations, and individuals involved in the design, manufacturing, testing, packaging, and distribution of semiconductors. The semiconductor supply chain typically involves several stages, which will often include:
- Design and development: Some semiconductor companies, also referred to as “fabless” companies, design and develop new chips, either in-house or through collaborations with other companies. They are called fabless because they do not themselves fabricate the chips that they design and market.
- Fabrication: The actual manufacturing of the semiconductor chips is done by specialized factories called foundries. The foundries receive chip designs from the fabless companies, and they use custom equipment to create and etch chips onto a silicon wafer.
- Testing and assembly: After the chips are manufactured, they need to be tested to ensure that they are functioning properly. This is typically carried out by separate companies that specialize in testing and assembly. Once the chips have passed the requisite tests, they are assembled into products that can be used in electronics and other devices.
- Distribution: The packaged chips are then distributed to the companies that will either sell them to end users or incorporate them into their products, either directly or through distributors.
In addition to these main stages, the semiconductor supply chain may also include intellectual property (IP) licensing, disposal, and recycling.
All of these stages require logistics and supply chain management, which also includes inventory management, order fulfillment, and transportation logistics. Efficient logistics and supply chain management are critical to ensure that the chips are delivered to the end users on time and in good condition.
Challenges and Vulnerabilities in the Semiconductor Supply Chain
The semiconductor supply chain has become increasingly complex over the past several decades. This complexity has also made the supply chain vulnerable to disruptions, as issues or bottlenecks at one stage of the chain can have ripple effects through the entire system. These can include natural disasters; for example, in 2011, a major earthquake and tsunami in Japan disrupted the global supply chain for semiconductors, leading to shortages and sharp price increases.5
One of the most significant disruptions to the semiconductor supply chain in recent years was the COVID-19 pandemic that struck in early 2020, which caused widespread lockdowns and disruptions to global shipping and logistics. Lockdowns caused worker shortages, and companies at all stages were forced to reduce capacity or temporarily shut down. This led to shortages of chips in many industries. Car manufacturers were particularly hurt by these disruptions, which had the knock-on effect of creating a shortage of new cars, which drove up the prices of used cars to record levels.6
Another factor contributing to the vulnerability of the semiconductor supply chain is the concentration of manufacturing in a few key regions, particularly in Asia. This concentration has made the supply chain susceptible to geopolitical tensions and trade disputes, which can disrupt the flow of materials and components. For example, the United States has placed trade restrictions on Chinese semiconductor companies to impede China’s military modernization by limiting access to the West’s most advanced chips, which have extensive military and advanced artificial intelligence applications. On January 13, 2026, the Commerce Department revised its policy to allow case-by-case licensing of certain chips for export to China under security conditions.789
 In addition to these external factors, the semiconductor supply chain has also experienced shortages due to internal factors, such as manufacturing capacity constraints and changes in demand, as the industry is characterized by long lead times and high capital investments. When demand exceeds supply, it can take months or even years for semiconductor manufacturers to build new foundries and ramp up production to meet the increased demand.
Strategies to Mitigate Semiconductor Supply Chain Disruptions
To better deal with supply chain disruptions, several steps can be undertaken, but they are neither particularly easy to implement nor inexpensive. For instance, increasing production capacity and diversifying the available suppliers to reduce reliance on any one company or region requires careful planning and coordination—along with billions of dollars of investment. Likewise, companies could invest more heavily in research and development (R&D) to develop new technologies and processes to make chips quickly and more efficiently, but this would also take a great deal of time and money.
Because of this, governments can help defray some of those costs by offering incentives and tax breaks, and can help coordinate the establishment of new domestic production facilities. The Biden administration hosted semiconductor industry gatherings to spur collaboration and has created the Supply Chain Disruptions Task Force to mitigate semiconductor supply chain disruptions.10
These efforts seem to be working. Intel broke ground in 2021 on two new foundries in Chandler, Ariz.—a $20 billion investment—along with an advanced packaging facility in New Mexico.1112 Micron, another large chip maker, has also invested $15 billion to add memory chip fabrication facilities to its headquarters in Boise, Idaho.1314 GlobalFoundries, Samsung Foundry, Texas Instruments, and Taiwan Semiconductor are all building new fabs in the U.S. due to these efforts.
In addition to these efforts, consulting firm Deloitte warns that by the year 2030, more than one million additional skilled workers will be needed to meet demand in the semiconductor industry. To preempt a supply chain disruption caused by a talent shortfall, they advocate building new talent pools in new locations and leveraging educational and community partnerships as never before.15
What Is the Outlook for the Semiconductor Supply Chain?
Despite unprecedented supply chain disruptions in the semiconductor sector following the COVID-19 pandemic, the outlook for the industry is looking better. In response to the shortages, companies and governments alike have expanded capacity, sought more diverse suppliers, and streamlined operations. However, it will take some time before this additional capacity comes online and the full effect of these measures is felt by consumers.
