TSMC Weighs Rare-Earth-Free Motors Amid China's Export Controls, Moves to Diversify Supply Chain [Taiwan Chip News]
TSMC Considers Replacing Rare-Earth Motors
Export Controls Threaten Semiconductor Component Supply Chains
Taiwanese Companies Pursue Alternative Technologies
Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s largest foundry, is considering adopting rare-earth-free motors to reduce supply chain risks arising from China’s export restrictions on rare earths. As even key components used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment become targets for supply chain diversification, Taiwanese companies are accelerating the development and commercialization of alternative technologies.
According to Taiwan’s Economic Daily News, Reuters and other sources on October 31, TSMC recently asked suppliers whether rare-earth-free motors could be used in its factory automation equipment. The move is intended to prepare for possible disruptions to component procurement caused by China’s export restrictions on rare earths. TSMC is including components that use rare earths in its equipment supply chain risk management and assessing whether they can be replaced.
In April 2025, China imposed export controls on items related to seven rare earths: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium. In October of the same year, it announced measures to further expand the controls to cover additional rare earths, as well as related equipment and technologies. The scope of the controls extended beyond rare-earth materials to include technologies related to permanent magnet manufacturing, increasing uncertainty across global supply chains.
China postponed until November 10, 2026, the implementation of some measures announced in October to expand the controls. However, existing export controls remain in place, increasing the need for companies to diversify their supply chains. Since rare earths are key materials for high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, robots and industrial automation equipment, the semiconductor industry is also closely monitoring their potential impact on the procurement of manufacturing equipment components. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that “defense and semiconductor supply chains could also be particularly affected if export licenses for components containing rare earth elements are delayed or denied.”
Adopting rare-earth-free motors requires more than simply replacing the magnets in existing motors. Their efficiency, torque, control performance and reliability must also meet the requirements of semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
In response, semiconductor component companies in Taiwan are drawing on their respective strengths in materials, motor design, and drive and control technologies to develop alternatives. As uncertainty over rare-earth supplies spills over into procurement challenges for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, companies are moving to secure related technologies and component supply chains ahead of time. China Steel is pursuing the development of alternative motors based on its materials technologies, including electrical steel sheets, while Fukuta is drawing on its motor design and manufacturing expertise. Shuo Yang is exploring ways to apply motor technologies that do not use rare-earth magnets, such as reluctance motors, in industrial equipment and cooling systems for AI data centers.
The Taiwanese government is also working to establish a domestic rare-earth supply chain. The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) currently operates a rare-earth pilot production line and, with government support, is moving forward with plans to build a separate demonstration production facility. The facility is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, with annual production of 500 tons of rare earths by the end of 2030. The Taiwanese government plans to use it to meet about 50% of the island’s domestic demand for rare earths.

Fraunhofer IIS integrated permanent micromagnets directly into the silicon substrate of a magnetic sensor chip at wafer level.

articles.title: DOJ charges California man with smuggling $300 million in Nvidia chips to China - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: DOJ charges California man with smuggling $300 million in Nvidia chips to China  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
A federal indictment unsealed this month accuses a California server reseller of running restricted Nvidia GPUs through Malaysia and Singapore to Chinese buyers. It's the exact route Malaysian customs had already caught in action this year.
On October 1, the Justice Department unsealed a three-count indictment against Greg Lui. He is the 38-year-old owner of Earthmade Computer Inc. in City of Industry, California. Prosecutors say Lui and his co-conspirators bought servers loaded with Nvidia A100 and H100 chips, plus GeForce RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 cards, from US manufacturers. The paperwork named approved overseas buyers as the final destination.
The hardware allegedly never stayed there.
According to the indictment, it moved through Malaysia and Singapore and ended up in China, where none of it was ever supposed to go without a Commerce Department licence. The numbers in the filing are specific enough to check. Take one transaction prosecutors cite: 27 servers bought for roughly $7.6 million in January 2024 and shipped to Kuala Lumpur. A co-conspirator later confirmed to Lui that the gear had been forwarded on to a Chinese buyer. Over the course of 2024, Earthmade allegedly took in more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipping companies. Prosecutors say that was part of a scheme that moved close to $300 million in restricted hardware between October 2023 and August 2026. That's according to the Department of Justice and reporting from Courthouse News and The Register.
Lui faces three charges: conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and outbound smuggling. The first two carry up to 20 years each. The smuggling count carries up to 10. He was arrested October 1 and, as of reporting by The Register and Newsweek, the case is pending in federal court.
Taipei is replacing its Huawei-and-SMIC blacklist with a blanket restriction on all Chinese buyers, backed by new criminal penalties under the Foreign Trade Act, following a $250 billion US trade pact signed in January. - taiwan AI chip export controls to China - smuggling advanced semiconductors criminal penalties Taiwan China
You don't have to take the indictment's word for how this works: Malaysian customs demonstrated it live five months earlier. On June 5, officers raided the free trade zone at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. They seized 72 server units worth about 52.9 million ringgit, roughly $12.9 million, declared as plain "computer components." The paperwork listed Malaysia as a transit point before the servers moved on to another Asian country. That would have required a permit under the country's Strategic Trade Act - and nobody had filed one. A Malaysian company tied to the shipment was brought in to assist the investigation.
That seizure wasn't an isolated catch. Malaysia had already opened a separate probe into how servers carrying US-made Nvidia chips, bound for Singapore, ended up on Malaysian soil instead. In July the government responded. It began requiring a Strategic Trade Permit, with immediate effect, for any export, transshipment, or transit of high-performance US-origin AI chips. Companies now have to give 30 days' notice under Section 12 of the Strategic Trade Act before moving anything on the restricted list through the country.
That is exactly what those rules were built to stop. The Lui indictment alleges it kept happening anyway, on a bigger scale than one airport seizure. Malaysian officials have said repeatedly that they've found no direct evidence of chip diversion through the country. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has said the same.
The DOJ's case argues otherwise, at least for this one network. And it puts a dollar figure on it that's more than twenty times the June seizure.
None of this makes Malaysia uniquely compromised. It makes Malaysia the hub where the paper trail happens to be checkable. Its export-control regime is new enough to still generate headlines when it catches something - or fails to. Singapore shows up in the same indictment with none of the same scrutiny, and that asymmetry is a story worth watching in its own right. The $176 million in payments from Malaysian shipping companies to one California reseller didn't move because Malaysia has lax rules on paper. It moved because enforcement, everywhere along that chain, lagged the volume of hardware looking for a way around a licence requirement.
Frankly, the chip war's black market has got big. Big enough that federal prosecutors now treat a single reseller's shipping records as a $300 million case, not a customs footnote. That's the real shift here - more than any one seizure or indictment on its own.

articles.title: Starlink outages in Ukraine have highlighted Europe’s critical dependence on US technology, - Bloomberg - Цензор.НЕТ
articles.summary: Starlink outages in Ukraine have highlighted Europe’s critical dependence on US technology, - Bloomberg  Цензор.НЕТ
articles.full_text:
Disruptions in the operation of the Starlink network in Ukraine have once again highlighted the European continent’s heavy reliance on American technology solutions. This incident has sparked renewed discussion about developing Europe’s own satellite capabilities, which would ensure the continent’s autonomy in the areas of critical communications and the defense sector.
This was reported by Censor.NET, citing Bloomberg.
Starshield Malfunctions and the Vulnerability of Ukrainian UAVs on the Front Lines
Disruptions to the military version of Starlink (Starshield) have highlighted Europe’s vulnerability and the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ dependence on U.S. space capabilities. These disruptions have hampered the operations of strike and interceptor drones on the front lines, while European partners still lack alternative satellite solutions for their armed forces.
The publication emphasizes that Europe’s dependence on the U.S. extends beyond Starlink: the EU does not have its own infrared systems for detecting missile launches and relies on U.S. space monitoring. This poses serious risks, as Europe’s defense capabilities are dependent on decisions made by Washington and U.S. private companies, making the issue of the EU’s technological autonomy extremely pressing.
The IRIS² Project and Alternatives
To reduce its dependence on foreign providers, the European Union is developing its own satellite network, IRIS², designed to ensure secure communications for government agencies, the defense sector, and critical infrastructure. The EU launched the first limited services under IRIS² and GOVSATCOM for military and government needs in early 2026, but the full-scale launch of individual services is not expected until at least 2029.
The alternative OneWeb network, operated by the European company Eutelsat, currently lags behind Starlink in terms of bandwidth, price, and equipment specifications for frontline use; moreover, Starlink terminals are not compatible with this system. Against this backdrop, some EU countries, notably Germany, are simultaneously deploying their own national satellite constellations.
Despite launching its own initiatives, Europe is currently unable to fully replace American satellite solutions. Starlink is significantly ahead of its competitors in terms of network scale and infrastructure complexity, and integrating alternative platforms requires substantial financial resources, time, and the replacement of terminals.
Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defense and Space, confirmed the continent’s high level of dependence on the U.S. space sector, emphasizing the need to strengthen its own technologies and cooperation within the EU.
Thus, the incidents involving Starlink have provided additional momentum for Europe’s push toward technological autonomy. However, over the next few years, European countries will still rely on U.S. communications and missile threat monitoring services while simultaneously developing their own equivalents.
Restrictions on Starlink Service in Ukraine
- On October 14, volunteer and former advisor to the Minister of Defense Serhiy Sternenko stated that overnight, SpaceX restricted the operation of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military. As a result, he said, "a number of important missions were disrupted." The restrictions were imposed on data transmission based on the speed of the UAVs using Starlink.
- Sergey Beskrestnov (Flash) later confirmed this information. According to him, the restrictions could also complicate the use of drones designed to intercept jet-powered suicide drones.
- Units of the 7th Corps of the Airborne Forces also reported that they began experiencing issues with Starlink connectivity in the Huliaipole area last night. This refers to the Starshield package—the so-called military package—which previously had no data transfer speed limits.
- Later, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov stated that the network is being restored to speeds of up to 160 km/h.
- At the same time, Elon Musk stated that he is not the one who sets the limits for Starshield, which Ukraine is using. This system is controlled by the U.S. government, not SpaceX.
- According to Reuters, the White House issued an order imposing restrictions on Starshield for Ukraine.
- On October 16, U.S. President Trump stated that Washington was not involved in the delay of the "military package" of Starlink (Starshield) satellite communications for the Ukrainian military.
- On October 19, Zelenskyy reported that in various sectors of the front, Ukrainian military vehicles equipped with the Starlink system stop functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour.
- Hegset stated that the Pentagon had not issued any orders to restrict Starshield.
- Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine, and on Thursday, Trump said that "the main thing is that he reversed everything" and declined to comment on whether he had called Musk.
- On October 22, Trump refused to say whether he had called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk regarding the speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- According to Politico, as of Friday morning, October 23, the Ukrainian military was still facing speed restrictions on Starlink, even though Trump had announced that the service had resumed full operation.
- On October 24, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense announced that SpaceX’s Starlink terminals and their military variants, StarShield, are once again operating at speeds exceeding 161 km/h. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed the resumption of Starlink service for Ukraine.

articles.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11214-yAn experimental concept enabling attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone is demonstrated and used to visualize the lightwave-driven electron motion of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta8,20. Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
According to the adiabatic theorem, a time-dependent, two-level quantum system remains in its ground state during a slow evolution21. By contrast, driving the system faster than its intrinsic timescale through an avoided energy crossing can create a finite occupation of the excited state by means of non-adiabatic transitions called Landau–Zener–Majorana (LZM) tunnelling22,23,24. This mechanism is central for strong-field light–matter interaction7,10,25,26. Yet, a direct observation of this foundational quantum effect in momentum space is still missing. The unique properties of graphene27 form the ideal test bed for observing LZM transitions. Its quasirelativistic electron dispersion and the robustness under irradiation with intense light have made this material a prime test ground for lightwave electronics26,28, including the demonstration of the first lightwave electronic logic gates7 and Floquet–Bloch states18,19. This has opened revolutionary prospects for quantum control, quantum sensing and quantum computation applications10,11,29.
Understanding and shaping the opportunities offered by lightwave control of electrons requires a direct observation of how LZM transitions dictate strong-field light–matter interaction. Attosecond spectroscopy has reached sufficient temporal resolution to access these dynamics30,31, and time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (trARPES) in combination with momentum microscopy32 has visualized electron dynamics directly in the band structure of quantum materials or in the orbitals of molecular layers12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,33. trARPES with subcycle temporal resolution8,20 has combined these approaches but offered only limited 1D momentum space access. To track coherent strong-field phenomena and scattering-induced momentum redistribution, observing carrier dynamics across the entire momentum space is imperative.
Here we expand subcycle band-structure videography to the entire first Brillouin zone (BZ). The new platform overcomes previous restrictions of momentum microscopy and subcycle ARPES, increasing the momentum area accessible with subcycle resolution by more than two orders of magnitude and the available field strengths by one order of magnitude. Exploiting few-cycle mid-infrared (MIR) field transients with large peak amplitudes, we drive coherent electron dynamics at the BZ edge of graphene. This approach reveals the simultaneous displacement and distortion of the light-driven electron distribution, uncovering the interplay between coherent intraband and interband dynamics underlying LZM transitions in graphene. Moreover, tracking the non-thermal subcycle distributions in 2D momentum space reveals how different scattering processes affect lightwave-driven dynamics.
Subcycle lightwave currents
When low-intensity, short-wavelength light interacts with electrons in a solid, it can induce perturbative interband quantum jumps in momentum regions in which the occupied and unoccupied bands are separated by an integer multiple of the photon energy (Fig. 1a). In graphene, the non-trivial pseudospin texture influences the dipole moments between the lower and upper halves of the Dirac cone, leading to a distribution of excited carriers only along the direction orthogonal to the light field34,35. Conversely, a strong low-frequency field transient can adiabatically accelerate carriers within their bands on subcycle timescales, deflecting the Fermi surface in momentum space according to Bloch’s acceleration theorem (Fig. 1b). During their excursion, electrons experience an energy gap, which, in graphene, varies linearly near the K point to form an avoided crossing. Thus, field-driven acceleration may drive prototypical LZM transitions, which leave a markedly different occupation in momentum space compared with Fig. 1a. If the driving field is periodic, the phase accumulated between consecutive non-adiabatic events—the Stückelberg phase—results in so-called Landau–Zener–Stückelberg–Majorana (LZSM) interference36,37.
To access this regime, we drive electrons in epitaxially grown monolayer graphene on SiC (ref. 38) with intense phase-stable MIR pulses (central frequency, 30 THz). After a delay time, t, extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses (central photon energy, 21.7 eV) photoemit the electrons with subcycle resolution. Their energies and momenta are detected with a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope (Fig. 1c and Methods). In equilibrium, the photoemission signal maps the occupied band structure. The high XUV photon energy and the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope capture the electronic structural dynamics throughout the entire first BZ, including its six corners, in a single measurement with sub-10-fs resolution.
Figure 2a shows several momentum distribution maps in the vicinity of a K point at selected energies. The in-plane component of the p-polarized XUV radiation driving the photoemission process is set parallel to the kx-axis. Owing to the matrix elements in the photoemission process, the intensity exhibits the characteristic horseshoe-like distribution for energies far below the Dirac point39. The influence of the dark corridor at ky = 0 and positive kx − K values is suppressed for energies close to the Dirac point, ED, and the photoemission intensity forms a disc. To ensure that the relevant dynamics occur along a direction in which the two branches of the Dirac cone have equal photoemission intensities, we apply an s-polarized MIR field along the ky-axis. For large negative delays (t = −70 fs), a slice of the photoelectron intensity for kx − K = 0 (Fig. 2b) shows two linear bands with a slope of ħvF (with the Fermi velocity vF = 10.7 Å fs−1) and a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point. With increasing t, we observe an apparent shift of the overall band structure owing to momentum streaking20 of photoemitted electrons in vacuo by the MIR field. This effect can be used to retrieve the MIR waveform at the sample surface (Extended Data Fig. 2a and Methods). Compensating for this shift isolates the subcycle electron dynamics within the band structure.
A corresponding femtosecond snapshot of the band structure for t = −13.6 fs shows a highly non-thermal lightwave-driven electron distribution (Fig. 2b). In the upper half of the Dirac cone (E − ED ≥ 0), the ky > 0 branch is occupied up to about 1 eV, whereas the ky  0, located perpendicular to the polarization of the incident light (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By contrast, the coupled intraband and interband dynamics of the LZM scenario leads to the observed unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field (Extended Data Fig. 6b). Simulations with varying field strengths confirm that this feature is characteristic of the strong-field regime (Extended Data Fig. 7).
The region in which LZM-type tunnelling can occur is determined by the field strength, E0, and the energy gap, which increases linearly with |kx − K|. This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models



When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.



He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.



Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.



—Matthew King



Are we there yet? Interspecies communication 



Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. 



Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.



Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.



—Cassandra Willyard



This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.



MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon



The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.



A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.



That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.



This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s websiteThe FEC filing system went offline a week before the midterms. (Reuters $)+ The attack is hiding spending data during the costliest midterms ever. (Gizmodo)+ Social media platforms are struggling to contain AI election lies. (Guardian)+ Software flaws in US voting machines threaten election security. (Axios)+ A blueprint for using AI to strengthen democracy. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Starlink restrictions have driven US allies to rethink their dependenceRestrictions in Ukraine have spooked officials across Europe. (Bloomberg $)+ And given European firms a new pitch for their rival services. (Axios)+ An Israeli spy firm allegedly targeted Starlink users. (Reuters $)+ Stratospheric internet could take off this year. (MIT Technology Review)



3 Greenhouse gas levels keep reaching new records worldwideCarbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide are all on the up. (New Scientist $)+ Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane. (Verge)+ The IPCC is fighting for survival. (Nature)+ How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. (MIT Technology Review)



4 Monkeys’ brains have revealed new clues about consciousnessTheir neural activity encodes images that escape their awareness. (Nature)+ Bees’ feelings are also changing views of consciousness. (New Scientist $)+ Debates over AI consciousness are a trap. (MIT Technology Review)



5 Chinese scientists have developed a catalyst to make Mars rocket fuelIt converts Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide into liquid methanol. (SCMP)



6 Tech billionaires have teamed up against California’s wealth taxSergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, and others have funded a major campaign. (NYT $)



7 Delaware plans to let AI agents run entire businessesThe proposal could let owners evade responsibility for harm. (Ars Technica)+ A better web for AI agents could hurt humans. (MIT Technology Review)



8 Palmer Luckey has unveiled plans for American-made military laptopsAnduril will build rugged PCs in Ohio using Qualcomm chips. (WSJ $)



9 Gen Z is turning away from the social media it grew up withYoung people are fueling a boom in digital detox tools. (Guardian)



10 Trump now wants to ban the term “artificial intelligence”He’s demanding we all start using “Super Intelligence.” (Gizmodo)



Quote of the day



“For the next two years, we’re going to be living in a state where, on average, every week there is a critical, internet-wide vulnerability.”



—Matthew Prince, Cloudflare’s chief executive, tells the New York Times that AI is currently finding software vulnerabilities quicker than they can be patched.



One more thing







Inside the controversial tree farms powering Apple’s carbon-neutral goal



In 2020, Apple set a goal to become net zero by the end of the decade. To hit that target, the company is offsetting its emissions by planting millions of eucalyptus trees in Brazil.



Apple is betting that the strategy will lead to a greener future. But critics warn that the industrial tree farms will do more harm than good.



Here’s why the plans have sparked a backlash.



—Gregory Barber

articles.full_text:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World
Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.
Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.
I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.
Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]
We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.
Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

articles.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
articles.summary: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. articles.full_text:
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.








DOWNLOAD THE REPORT




An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.







Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.



“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”







The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.



Download the report

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time



—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.



AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. 



As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.



​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. 



Here’s what needs to change.



Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot



Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.



Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.



Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming.



—James Temple



This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.



Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries 



Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.



The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.



Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.



—Alexander C. Kaufman



This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workersIncluding undercover ICE agents. (Wired $)+ Much of the data relates to Customs and Border Protection. (TechCrunch)+ It also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools. (Reuters $)+ Big Tech is pushing back against ICE’s demands for user data. (WSJ $)+ Activists want ChatGPT users to quit over ICE ties. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Putin says Russia is coordinating with “genius” Musk on satellitesHe said the cooperation maintains order in orbit. (Bloomberg $)+ ​​Russia is developing its own version of Starlink. (Guardian)+ Moscow added Apple and Microsoft to a surveillance registry. (Quartz)+ Here’s all the stuff we’ve put up in space. (MIT Technology Review)



3 Apple just announced its first-ever MacBook with a touchscreenIt joins a blitz of product launches under new CEO John Ternus. (CNN)+ Steve Jobs and Tim Cook had both dismissed the idea. (NYT $)+ Executives say touchscreen advances mean it’s now worthwhile. (Wired $)



4 Bloomberg and trading firms are paying to get Trump’s posts fasterThey’ve signed up for Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan. (Reuters $)



5 As US ties fray, Europe is planning its first subsea cable to GreenlandIt will bypass the US to link Canada, Japan, and South Korea. (Ars Technica)+ The EU’s AI champion says Europe can rival US tech giants. (FT $)



6 Palantir’s defense chief says AI could make China target TaiwanHe says Beijing may act to stop the US pulling ahead in AI. (Bloomberg $)+ Taiwan’s “silicon shield” could be weakening. (MIT Technology Review)



7 Musk’s xAI has offered to buy homes if residents drop a noise lawsuitThe suit targets noise from powering its Mississippi data centres. (Guardian)



8 The world’s first spinal cord transplant has sparked controversyExperts say there’s little evidence the operation will work. (New Scientist $)



9 China’s tech giants are fighting for attention with AI microdramasTencent and ByteDance are battling over the booming market. (SCMP)+ Chinese microdramas are AI content machines. (MIT Technology Review)



10 Astronomers have spotted a possible new dwarf planet beyond PlutoThe icy world would be the solar system’s sixth dwarf planet. (Gizmodo)



Quote of the day



“They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” 



—A hacking group explains why it leaked personal information from the US Department of Homeland Security, NPR reports.



One more thing







How the Pentagon is adapting to China’s technological rise



It’s been just over a year since Kathleen Hicks stepped down as US deputy secretary of defense.



As the highest-ranking woman in Pentagon history, Hicks shaped US military posture through an era defined by renewed competition between powerful countries and a scramble to modernize defense technology.



In this conversation with MIT Technology Review, Hicks reflects on how the Pentagon is adapting—or failing to adapt—to a new era of geopolitical competition. She discusses China’s technological rise, the future of AI in warfare, and her signature initiative: Replicator. 



Check out the full interview.



—Caiwei Chen



We can still have nice things



A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)



+ Astronomers have found a green star 280 light-years from Earth.+ A Scottish labrador that detects “sea vomit” has won the Animal of the Year award.+ England’s iconic Sycamore Gap is showing signs of new life three years on from its felling.+ From Lime-bike jousting to chainmail-wearing pop stars, youth culture is embracing the medieval era.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.summary: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem…
articles.full_text:
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. 



AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. 



Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.



As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.





Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.



With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. 



The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.



Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.



Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it. 



OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.



Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.



No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety. 



AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist. 



Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research. 



No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.



Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.



Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

articles.full_text:
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.



Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.





A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. 



None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.



A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.



Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group. 



At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.



But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue. 





So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions. 



Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.



Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations. 



The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels. 



This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

articles.title: An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War
articles.summary: An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about.
articles.full_text:
Listen to this post:













Good morning,



Today’s Stratechery Interview is with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar. Sankar has worked at Palantir for 20 years, and has taken on an increasingly visible role as public intellectual, including authoring the book Mobilize, an exhortation “To Reboot the American Industrial Base and Stop World War III”. I previously interviewed Sankar in June 2023. That interview is a great place to start in terms of understanding Palantir, which we mostly discuss in this interview in the context of AI.



To that end, in this interview we discuss why Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion, why companies focused on the top-line have more success adopting AI, and why he is frustrated at the labs refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety. Then we discuss what Palantir has learned from AI, how companies can preserve alpha instead of the median, and whether or not we need more models. Sankar also explains exactly what a forward-deployed engineer is, why tech is in a religious war, and his retrospective on Anthropic’s battle with the U.S. government.



This Interview is presented by Stripe, the economic infrastructure of AI, and for Stratechery itself.



As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.



On to the Interview:



An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War



This interview is lightly edited for clarity.



Topics:
Diffusing Intelligence | Top Line vs. Bottom Line | Safety and Systems Engineering | Palantir’s AI Lessons | Alpha vs. Beta | Model Questions | Forward-Deployed Engineering | Anthropic vs. the U.S. Government | AI Religion



Background



Shyam Sankar, welcome back to Stratechery.



SS: Ben, thanks for having me back.



Well, the last time we talked was in conjunction with Ted Mabrey, the head of Palantir Commercial. As is usually the case with dual interviews, we got right down to business — and I do have to say, I do a lot of interviews where I usually kind of know where I want to go, but that one was super helpful to me in understanding Palantir and thinking about AI generally. But before we get into that, we never got to do my traditional background questions — where you came from, how you got to where you are. So for you, do we start in Orlando, in Lagos, or in India?



SS: At least Lagos. My father, in his early 20s, moved to Lagos and built one of the first pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities in all of Africa. He set up this whole life there for the better part of ten years. I was born in India, but really I grew up until I was three in Lagos.



And then there was this horrible armed robbery that happened at the house — they decapitated the dog, pistol-whipped my father, and threatened my mother. So we left all of our earthly possessions behind and started over again in Orlando, which ended up being a truly phenomenal place to grow up. The profound optimism of Disney World, the shadow of the Space Coast, seeing shuttle launches in elementary school, running into your courtyard filled with this sense of optimism about how technology will inevitably lead to a better world — which, if you fast-forward twenty years from the ’80s, I think kids were fed a very different diet of Terminator and “nature always finds a way“, “How dare man try to do anything that creates progress?”, so that’s really where it started.



Is that actually the ultimate example of man overcoming nature — not the space shuttle, but in fact Disney World?



SS: (laughing) That’s true! The fact that millions of people go there every year, to the middle of the swamp — and it’s fantastic, a lot of fun.



What does meritocracy mean to you? I was reading the recent profile of you in Colossus, and it opened with [Palantir CEO] Alex Karp’s statements in that regard, but it was put in the context of you growing up in Orlando, taking an entrance exam to go to Trinity High School, and how that launched you into what you became. Is that a sentiment from Alex, is it from you, or what’s your take?



SS: It’s a sentiment for both of us, for different reasons. We’re both kind of acquired tastes, in many ways, and living in a world that judges you by the fruits you bear, rather than any dimension you have no control over, is obviously a better world to live in. I think it’s a precondition to the American Dream.



I was going to ask you that. Because you have this background — born in India, originally living in Lagos, come to America. What does being an American mean to you? Is that the same question, or is there some tension between those two things?



SS: They overlap profoundly. Being an American is this profound belief in your own human agency, and the community you’re in, and the ability to create a more perfect union — the recognition, the ability to hold the contradiction, that not everything is perfect today but it’s incumbent on us to make it better. That may sound a little Pollyannish and even corny, but that doesn’t exist anywhere else. Everywhere else, people are profoundly cynical — things are the way they are — and there’s a very thin line between cynicism and nihilism, and you kind of give up on everything. That’s the death spiral, that’s how you get the Dark Ages.



After university and graduate school, you worked on Xoom, on remittances — and then you go to work for Palantir.



SS: Xoom with an X.



Xoom with an X, that’s right. Not the Zoom with a Z — which maybe I shouldn’t be talking to, since you’re now an executive at Palantir using Zoom with a Z, but that’s another discussion. You worked on Xoom and remittances, then Palantir, working on national security, arguing for building our homegrown industrial base. There’s an argument there that — to take a paradox that’s maybe unfair — how do you go from a career focused on sending money out of America to being an advocate for money here in America, rebuilding our capital base? Is there tension there, or am I creating paradoxes out of thin air to build a theme?



SS: I think you’re creating a bit of a paradox out of thin air. First of all, there’s a policy question — if you have a working class trying to get money to support their family, how can they do that as efficiently as possible?



The bigger issue is the profound lie of globalization. The calculus that globalization got wrong is this idea that we can do the innovation and “they” can do the production — “they” make the things, we do the innovation. The problem is that innovation is a consequence of productivity, if you stop making the thing, you cede the stimulus required to do the innovation around the thing.



The example I always give young computer scientists is, what do you think motivated Google to do the research behind “Attention Is All You Need“? If you talk to that team, they wanted the 3% improvement in Google Translate. You cannot think of something more prosaic leading to something more profound. So we should be very careful where we give up — we buy a little too much into comparative advantage and give up the stimulus for production.



Why do you think — what leads to that mistake of thinking that it’s okay to just own the inputs and not worry about the outputs?



SS: Because at the margin, it’s true. At the margin, you can hire WuXi as a cheap set of hands at the lab bench to do a little bit of work. But at the limit, that’s a transfer of knowledge. At every increment it seems to make sense — you’re still doing the innovation — until one day you wake up and realize, “Oh, I don’t have it anymore”.



Diffusing Intelligence



You’re the only Stratechery interview that I’ve offered a job to. You sent over a list of questions you wanted me to talk about, and I have to say they’re really good — I did ask if you wanted to prepare all my interviews going forward, I don’t think I got a response, maybe the email got lost.



SS: (laughing) I’m thinking about it.



Okay, good. Well, let’s drill in — we’ll take your outline, why not, go through it and talk about it, and I think there are themes that might emerge. Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!



As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone. Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.




Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers. Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon. After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday. Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet.— Andrew Sharp









The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine). Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions. First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years. But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives. As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take! — AS



Autocracies Then and Now. On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected. Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé. On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text, I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated. — AS









Presented by







When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe, because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.



Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms.



Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it.AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves.



No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.



GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.



A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue.



Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse.



—Jessica Hamzelou



This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.



Love is infrastructure



—“Love is Infrastructure” is a short fictional story by Charlie Jane Anders, author of a forthcoming novel titled Good Things Are Coming Your Way.



Mainspring and St. Barnabas are two neighboring cities with different personalities. They’ve never particularly liked each other, but that changes when both develop minds of their own, shaped by the votes of their residents.



As the cities begin to fall for each other, a third city enters the picture. Turnbull promises Mainspring a more efficient future, but its vision of urban life comes with a troubling price.



Read the full short story about self-aware cities, direct democracy, and a steamy romance.



This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.



Are we there yet? Cleaning up PFAS 



Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. 



Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. 



Find out how close we are to ridding the world of forever chemicals.

This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.

—Steven Strogatz, a mathematics professor at Cornell University, tells Business Insider that personal appeal will become more valuable as AI increasingly takes over intellectual work.

The Bay Area’s animal welfare movement wants to recruit AI



In early February, animal welfare advocates and AI researchers arrived in stocking feet at Mox, a shoes-free coworking space in San Francisco. They gathered to discuss a provocative idea: if artificial general intelligence is on the horizon, could it prevent animal suffering?



Some brainstormed using custom agents in advocacy work, while others pitched cultivating meat with AI tools. But the real talk of the event was a flood of funding they expect will soon flow to animal welfare charities, not from individual megadonors, but from AI lab employees.

articles.summary: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. articles.full_text:
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.



A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.





What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.



Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.



Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.



It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.



Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.



That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).



The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.





Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.



It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.



Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?



Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.



Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.



When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.



The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.





Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”



“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.



Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.



In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.



Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.



“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.



Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.



If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.

The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. articles.title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
articles.summary: Antarctic waters are getting saltier as sea-ice loss reshapes ocean circulation.
articles.full_text:
The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.
In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.
The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.Read full article
